title: Auto Transport Leads: How to Get Them and Pay Less (2026)
summary: How auto transport companies get leads: buy shared leads, run Google and Meta ads, and track cost per booked shipment. Examples from live ads.
body_markdown:
## The short answer


- Auto transport leads come from three places: bought shared leads, your own Google Search ads, and Meta ads that catch people before they start searching.
- Shared leads are fast but sold to several brokers at once. Your own ads cost more to set up and give you leads nobody else is calling.
- The ads that keep running ask if the car needs to move, promise a fast nationwide price and say carriers will bid, so the owner does not have to hunt.
- Measure cost per booked shipment, not cost per lead. A cheap lead that never answers the phone is the most expensive kind.


## What an auto transport lead is


An auto transport lead is a person who has a vehicle to move and has asked for a price. The form usually captures pickup and delivery location, vehicle year and make, whether it runs, open or enclosed trailer, and a target date. That is enough for a broker or carrier to quote.


The buyer is in a hurry and slightly annoyed. They are relocating, buying a car out of state, selling one online or sending a student off to school. They do not want a project. They want the car moved and the question closed. That shapes every part of lead generation in this trade: the faster and simpler the path to a price, the more leads you get.


It also means the buyer fills out more than one form. Most people request quotes from several companies in the same hour. Whoever calls first with a clear number has the best shot at the booking.


## Where auto transport leads come from


Every source trades cost against control. Here is how the main ones compare.


Bought shared leads Google Search ads Meta ads (Facebook and Instagram) Referrals and repeat


Who sees the lead You and several other companies You, plus a few competitors who also appear in the results Mostly you Only you


Speed to first lead Same day Days, once the account is set up Days, after the creative is approved Slow to build


Buyer intent High, but shopping around High, searching right now Medium, interrupted while scrolling Highest


Control over message None Full Full Full


Main risk Price war on the phone, duplicate leads Paying for clicks from people who want a different service Low-quality form fills from people not ready to ship Volume stays small


Most companies start with shared leads because they work on day one. Many then add their own ads once they see how much of the margin the lead vendor takes. The two can run side by side.


## A worked example: cost per booked shipment


Cost per lead is the number everyone quotes and the one that misleads. The number that matters is what you spend to book one shipment. The figures below are illustrations, not benchmarks. Replace them with your own.


Shared leads Own Google ads


Cost per lead $20 $35


Leads that answer the phone 50% 70%


Answered leads that book 20% 30%


Bookings per 100 leads 10 21


Spend per 100 leads $2,000 $3,500


Cost per booked shipment $200 $167


In this example the lead that costs 75 percent more ends up cheaper per booking. The reason is that you are the only one calling, so more people answer and more say yes. If your gross profit on a typical shipment is $300, the shared lead leaves $100 and the own-ad lead leaves $133. The gap compounds across a month of volume.


Your numbers will differ. The method does not. Count leads, answered calls, bookings and spend per source, then divide.


## What live auto transport ads show


The[auto transport ad wall](https://www.sprites.ai/auto-transport-ads) shows 12 advertisers running 47 ads on Meta. A little over four in ten of those ads are video, and the typical ad has been running about 50 days. The most common call to action is Get quote, used by roughly six in ten ads.


That tells you what this trade has settled on. The ad is short, the button is a quote, and the creative is often a person or a truck rather than a studio shot. A median run of 50 days means ads are tested and replaced quickly, while a few stay up for years.


The longest-running ads share a few traits:


- **They ask a plain question.** One that has run 344 days opens with "Moving cross-country? Don’t add car drama to the list." It names the situation the buyer is already in and treats the car as one more item to cross off.
- **They name the action.** Another, running 260 days, opens "🚗 Need to ship your car?" That is the whole pitch in five words, and the form is one tap away.
- **They offer a fast price.** The ads that last tend to promise a free quote, often nationwide, with a quick answer.
- **They explain how the price is found.** Several say carriers bid on the shipment, which tells the owner that they will not have to call around.
- **They sound like a company that will pick up.** The oldest ad on the page, over six years old, opens by describing a locally owned, minority-owned shipping company and where its office is. Another says, in effect, that the company does not overpromise and just delivers. Owners handing over a car want a reason to trust a stranger.


What you do not see in the ones that last is a long list of services or a discount code. The ad does one job and gets out of the way.


## Google Search for auto transport leads


Search catches people who have already decided to ship. Typical terms include "car shipping," "auto transport quotes," "ship a car to Florida" and "enclosed car transport." Route-based terms are narrower and often cheaper than broad ones.


A few rules keep the spend honest:


- Group ads by intent. Separate open transport, enclosed transport, military moves and dealer or auction shipping.
- Use negative keywords. Exclude "jobs," "driver," "how to become," "truck rental" and "tow." People searching those are not shipping a car.
- Send clicks to a page that opens with the quote form. Do not send them to a home page with a menu.
- Make the phone number tappable. Some buyers prefer to call, and a call that connects often books on the spot.


The same principles apply in a neighboring trade. Our guide to[Google Ads for moving companies](https://www.sprites.ai/google-ads-for-moving-companies) covers route terms and call tracking for a similar buyer.


## Meta ads for auto transport leads


Meta reaches people who have a move coming but have not searched yet. Think of someone who just accepted a job in another state or bought a car from a seller two states away. The ad has to do the work of getting their attention, so it should be blunt.


A simple structure that matches what the longer-running ads do:


1. **Opening line:** a question the buyer would say out loud. "Need to ship your car?" works.
2. **Middle:** one sentence on how the price works. "Carriers bid on your shipment. You get the best price without making a dozen calls."
3. **Close:** the button, Get quote, and a promise on timing, such as a price the same day.


Use a short instant form. Ask for pickup zip, delivery zip, vehicle and email or phone. Every extra field loses people, but one or two qualifying questions, such as whether the car runs and the move date, save your dispatcher from calling people who are months away. Video can be a person talking to the camera for 15 seconds or a clip of a carrier loading a car. Neither needs production work.


## Speed to lead decides who books


Buyers send several quote requests at once, so the first useful call usually wins. Set a target. Call within five minutes during business hours and text right away if the call goes unanswered. A text such as "Hi, this is Dana from \[Company\]. I have your quote for the Austin to Denver move. Do you have a minute?" gets more replies than a voicemail.


When you quote, give a number and a window. Vague answers lose to the competitor who says $950, pickup in 3 to 5 days. If your price is higher, say why: enclosed trailer, insurance coverage or a vetted carrier.


## Common mistakes that waste lead spend


- **Counting every form fill as a lead.** Remove duplicates, bad numbers and people who are only checking prices.
- **Quoting too low to win the click.** A bid that no carrier will take leads to cancellations and bad reviews.
- **Running one ad for every service.** A snowbird shipping to Arizona and a dealer moving ten cars need different messages.
- **Ignoring seasonality.** Demand rises with summer moves and snowbird routes. Raise budgets before the peak, not during it.
- **Never checking the account.** Budgets drift and search terms creep. Review weekly.

## FAQ


### What are auto transport leads?


They are people who have a vehicle to move and have requested a price. A lead normally includes pickup and delivery locations, vehicle details, trailer type and a target date, plus a phone number or email so you can respond.


### Should I buy auto transport leads or run my own ads?


Many companies do both. Bought leads give volume quickly but are shared with other companies, so you compete on the phone. Your own ads cost more to build but the leads are yours alone, which usually raises the share that answer and book. Compare the two by cost per booked shipment.


### What do the best auto transport ads say?


The longest-running ads on the[auto transport ad wall](https://www.sprites.ai/auto-transport-ads) ask if the car needs to move, offer a fast price and use Get quote as the button. Several explain that carriers bid on the shipment, which spares the owner from calling around.


### How fast should I respond to a lead?


Within five minutes during business hours. Buyers usually request quotes from several companies at once, and the first clear price tends to win. Follow a missed call with a text.


### How do I know if my leads are good?


Track the share that answer the phone, the share that book, and the cost per booked shipment for each source. A low cost per lead with a low booking rate is usually worse than a higher cost per lead that books often.
